name: artisan french bread
instructions:
1.5 tsp salt, 3 cups FLOUR TOTAL (see flour-composition note below), 1 tbsp yeast, 1 tsp sugar (to activate the yeast). Bake at 425°F.

HYDRATION: pour warm water from a cup for the bulk of it, then STOP POURING and finish with WET HANDS — get your hands wet and knead, re-wetting as needed, until the dough feels right (see WET-HANDS FINISH note; pouring to the end is how you overhydrate).

FLOUR COMPOSITION — 1 CUP AP IS ALWAYS NECESSARY (FOR BALANCE); THE OTHER 2 CUPS CAN BE AP / WHEAT / BREAD:
- 1 cup AP flour — non-negotiable, always in the mix for balance.
- The other 2 cups: AP, wheat, or bread flour — but DON'T MIX BREAD FLOUR AND WHEAT FLOUR in the same batch (they don't play well together; see notes). CAP WHEAT AT 1 CUP.
- Two favorite variants:
  - Variant A: 1 cup AP + 2 cups bread flour (chewy). If GLAZING, shape as SMALL ROLLS — see GLAZE note (the glaze, not the bread flour, is what causes the burned-crust / undercooked-interior problem on large loaves).
  - Variant B — RUSTIC WHEAT BREAD: 2 cups AP + 1 cup wheat.
notes:
Adapted from Julia Child (Mastering the Art of French Cooking).

FINALIZED RATIOS (THE CURRENT RECIPE): 1.5 tsp salt, 3 cups flour TOTAL (composition rules below), 1 tbsp yeast, 1 tsp sugar to activate the yeast. This is what I've landed on after iterating on Julia's original.

JULIA CHILD'S ORIGINAL: her original called for 2 tsp salt, 3.5 cups all-purpose flour, 2 tbsp wheat flour, and 1 tbsp yeast (no sugar to activate). I found that version came out too salty, too dense, and too plain. The adjustments I landed on:
- DROP SALT from 2 tsp → 1.5 tsp.
- YEAST: back to 1 tbsp (matches Julia's). Bumped this to 1.5 tbsp for a while trying to get more rise / less density, then walked it back — 1 tbsp is right.
- ADD 1 TSP SUGAR TO ACTIVATE THE YEAST. Not in Julia's original.
- REWORK THE FLOUR TOTAL AND COMPOSITION: 3 cups total (down from 3.5), with a flexible composition — see below. Superseded my previous 3 AP + 0.5 wheat landing.

=== FLOUR COMPOSITION — 1 CUP AP ALWAYS + 2 CUPS FLEXIBLE (AP / WHEAT / BREAD) ===

- 1 CUP AP FLOUR IS ALWAYS NECESSARY for balance. Non-negotiable — even in the more experimental variants, 1 cup of AP stays in the mix.
- THE OTHER 2 CUPS: AP, wheat, or bread flour — but NOT bread + wheat together (see next point).
- BREAD FLOUR AND WHEAT FLOUR DON'T MIX WELL: tried the three-way 1 AP + 1 wheat + 1 bread combination; walked back. The bread-flour chew and the wheat character fight each other rather than layering. Pick a lane: bread-flour variant (A) or wheat variant (B), not both in one batch.
- CAP WHEAT AT 1 CUP: 2 cups of wheat is too much — the wheat character takes over.
- Two favorite variants I've landed on:
  - VARIANT A: 1 cup AP + 2 cups bread flour. The bread flour bumps the gluten and chew. (An earlier note here blamed the bread flour for undercooked/gummy interiors in large loaves — that attribution was WRONG; the glaze was the culprit. See GLAZE CAUSES THE UNDERCOOKING note below.)
  - VARIANT B — RUSTIC WHEAT BREAD: 2 cups AP + 1 cup wheat. Replaces the old 1 AP + 1 wheat + 1 bread three-way (walked back per the bread+wheat rule above). The 2:1 AP-to-wheat lands the rustic wheat character on a clean AP base.

SALT — DON'T SECOND-GUESS THE 1.5 TSP: past experiments where the bread seemed 'too little salt' at 1.5 tsp were NOT actually caused by too-little salt. They were caused by OVERHYDRATING the dough (too much water) and then adding flour to compensate — which diluted the salt-to-flour ratio without reducing the water. The salt itself was fine; the ratio drifted because of the water-then-flour compensation. Real fix: hit the hydration right the first time (see WATER / HYDRATION below), don't chase salt as the correction.

If you want to taste the original alongside the adapted version sometime, run a side-by-side to confirm the changes are real. My memory of the original is that the differences are noticeable.

=== WATER / HYDRATION — POUR EARLY, WET-HANDS FINISH ===

From experience, 2 cups is way too much. 1 cup is probably not enough. Right number is in between somewhere — and it's hard to titrate precisely because the last bit of water is where the risk lives.

THE TECHNIQUE — WET-HANDS FINISH: start by pouring warm water into the dough from a cup — that's fine for the bulk of the hydration. But TOWARD THE END, STOP POURING. Dumping water directly into a nearly-hydrated dough is how you overshoot (and overhydration is the root failure behind the salt-ratio drift documented above). Instead, when the dough is still slightly UNDER-hydrated: GET YOUR HANDS WET and knead. Each wet-hands pass works a small, controlled amount of water into the dough — keep re-wetting and kneading until the dough FEELS right. The hands are the titration instrument; you physically can't overshoot the way a cup-pour can, and you're reading the dough's feel on every pass.

This converts the hydration problem from a measurement problem (what's the right number of cups?) into a feel problem (knead until it feels right) — which is the more reliable frame for bread dough anyway.

=== CRUST — TWO WAYS THAT WORK, PLUS THE PREFERRED HYBRID ===

I've found two crust techniques that work for this bread:

1. BOTTOM-OVEN-BOILING-WATER (STEAM) TECHNIQUE: place a pan of boiling water on the bottom rack of the oven while the bread bakes on the middle rack. The steam gives you the classic french-bread crackly crust.

2. EGG WASH OR EGG + CREAM WASH: brush the loaf/rolls with beaten egg (alone), or with a mix of egg + heavy cream, before baking. Gives you a shinier, browner crust than the steam method.

PREFERRED HYBRID — ROLL IN CREAM BY HAND, THEN BRUSH WITH EGG: the best practical technique I've landed on. ROLL the entire loaf/rolls in heavy cream using your hands — the hand-rolling covers every surface easily, no missed spots. Then brush beaten egg on top with a brush. Two advantages: (1) full cream coverage that a brush alone can't reliably deliver, (2) the cream helps SEEDS STICK if you're topping with sesame/pumpkin/sunflower/etc. before the egg goes on.

PURE CREAM (NO EGG) — WEAKER, BUT NOT A FAILURE: cream alone DOES make a crust — weaker than the egg or egg+cream versions, but real. Also helps seeds stick. So it's a valid fallback if you're out of eggs. Should have googled before running the experiment years ago (originally logged as a failure — updating now).

=== GLAZE CAUSES THE UNDERCOOKING PROBLEM — NOT THE BREAD FLOUR (CORRECTED ATTRIBUTION) ===

Correction to an earlier diagnosis: I previously blamed 2 cups of bread flour (variant A) for large loaves coming out with a burned crust and undercooked/gummy interior — while forgetting that I had GLAZED that batch. The real culprit is the EGG + CREAM GLAZE: the glaze browns the crust much faster than a bare or steam-baked loaf, so on a LARGE loaf the crust reads done (or burns) while the interior is still lagging behind. The bread flour was innocent.

RULE: IF YOU'RE GLAZING, MAKE THE ROLLS SMALLER. Smaller pieces cook through before the glazed crust over-browns. Large glazed loaves are the failure mode; large UNGLAZED (steam-technique) loaves are fine.

WANT TO TRY — ADD THE GLAZE PARTWAY THROUGH THE BAKE: instead of glazing before the loaf goes in, bake bare for the first stretch and brush the glaze on partway through. The interior gets a head start before the fast-browning glaze goes on — should let larger glazed formats work. Untested; log when tried.

=== SEEDS ON TOP — SESAME ONLY (FLAX IS TOO HEAVY) ===

Of the seeds I've tried topping this bread with, only SESAME SEEDS actually stick to the top well. The cream + egg wash holds sesame in place through the bake.

FLAX SEEDS ARE TOO HEAVY — FALL OFF: tried topping with flax seeds; they don't stick. Too heavy for the wash to hold. If you want the flax nutrition, put it INSIDE the dough instead of on top (want-to-try below).

WANT TO TRY — FLAX INSIDE + SESAME ON TOP: the hybrid I plan to try next. Flax seeds mixed into the dough (where their weight doesn't matter and they get physically bound in), sesame seeds scattered on top (where they actually stick with the wash). Untested; log when tried.
